content: Preventive chemotherapy (PC) is a strategy aimed at reducing the risk of infection in populations by achieving high levels of drug coverage. This strategy can be implemented in three distinct ways: 1. Mass Drug Administration (MDA): This involves administering PC at regular intervals to all eligible members of entire communities in geographical areas identified as being at risk, regardless of their infection status. 2. Targeted Chemotherapy: This approach administers PC at regular intervals but only to specific at-risk groups. 3. Selective Chemotherapy: This involves administering PC exclusively to individuals who have been screened for taeniasis infection and confirmed to be positive. Several anthelmintic drugs have demonstrated efficacy in treating taeniasis and are currently utilized in various settings. These include niclosamide (NICL), praziquantel (PZQ), and albendazole (ALB). All three drugs are listed as intestinal anthelmintics in the World Health Organization (WHO) Model List of Essential Medicines (21st List, 2019). PZQ, at a dose of 40 mg/kg, is used in PC programs for controlling schistosomiasis, clonorchiasis, and opisthorchiasis. ALB is routinely used in MDA and targeted PC programs to control soil-transmitted helminths (STH) at a single dose of 400 mg. However, the optimal drug and dose for PC to control Taenia solium (T. solium) taeniasis remain unknown. The 2005 FAO/WHO/OIE Guidelines for the Surveillance, Prevention, and Control of Taeniosis and Cysticercosis did not include recommendations for PC use against T. solium taeniasis. These guidelines were not based on systematic evidence reviews or the GRADE approach to guideline development. Consequently, program managers and stakeholders require clear, evidence-based guidance to select appropriate drugs for specific settings and to implement, monitor, and evaluate PC programs effectively. This new WHO guideline was developed to address these gaps and provide evidence-based recommendations for PC to control T. solium taeniasis. It is important to note that the treatment of neurocysticercosis is a separate, complex, and specialized subject, which is beyond the scope of this guideline. WHO has developed a separate guideline for the clinical management of T. solium neurocysticercosis. Objectives of the Guideline: 1. To provide evidence-based recommendations on the appropriate choice of drug(s) and dose for PC of T. solium in endemic areas. 2. To support WHO Member States in developing evidence-based national PC strategies for T. solium. 3. To inform a research priority agenda to generate new evidence that could strengthen future recommendations. Scope of the Guideline: The guideline focuses on PC for T. solium taeniasis in endemic human populations. It includes three commercially available anthelmintics—NICL, PZQ, and ALB—that have shown efficacy in treating taeniasis. The recommendations are based on systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and other studies, as well as the technical expertise of the Guideline Development Group (GDG), Steering Group, and External Review Group. Outcomes of Interest: Critical outcomes for decision-making include: Infection rate with T. solium taeniasis: Measured by cure rate (%) as an indicator of drug efficacy and relative reduction in prevalence (%) as an indicator of drug effectiveness in PC programs. Risk of side effects: Including serious neurological side effects (e.g., seizures or severe headaches) that may indicate exacerbation of undiagnosed or latent neurocysticercosis, as well as mild or moderate side effects. Other considerations: Observation time for side effects, cost-effectiveness, feasibility, preferences of affected populations, and impact on equity. When considering simultaneous treatment of T. solium taeniasis and STH in school-age children, additional outcomes include: Infection rate with STH. Risk of side effects from simultaneous administration of two medications. Target Audience: The guideline is intended for policymakers, technical and program staff, and researchers involved in planning, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating PC programs for T. solium control. It also aims to guide researchers in addressing evidence gaps that constrain the development of strong recommendations. Funding: The guideline was solely funded by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) and WHO, with no external funding from bilateral technical partners or industry. WHO Guideline Development Process: The guideline was developed using WHO’s standard methods, ensuring transparency between evidence and recommendations. The process involved five main groups: 1. WHO Guideline Steering Group: Responsible for overall coordination, drafting the scope, formulating key questions, and managing conflicts of interest. 2. Systematic Review Team: Conducted systematic reviews, evaluated evidence quality using GRADE, and drafted Evidence to Decision frameworks. 3. Guideline Development Group (GDG): A diverse group of 19 members, including external experts and stakeholders from endemic countries, who developed evidence-based recommendations. 4. External Review Group: Reviewed the draft guideline for errors, clarity, and implementation implications without altering recommendations. 5. WHO Guideline Review Committee: Ensured high-quality, evidence-based, and transparent guideline development. Key Research Questions: 1. Should PC with NICL, PZQ, or ALB, at any dose or frequency, versus no PC, be used for controlling T. solium taeniasis in endemic populations? Population: People in T. solium-endemic areas. Intervention: PC with NICL, PZQ, or ALB at varying doses and frequencies. Comparison: No PC. Outcomes: Infection rate with T. solium taeniasis, side effects (including neurological effects), and observation time for side effects. 2. In school-age children in areas co-endemic with T. solium and STH, could PC for these parasites be administered simultaneously? Population: School-age children in co-endemic areas. Intervention: Simultaneous PC with NICL or PZQ for taeniasis and ALB for STH. Comparison: Separate administration of NICL or PZQ for taeniasis and ALB for STH. Outcomes: Infection rates for STH and T. solium taeniasis, and risk of side effects from simultaneous medication. Systematic Review: The evidence informing the recommendations was based on a systematic review conducted as part of the guideline development process. Eligible study designs included RCTs, non-randomized controlled trials, and economic evaluations. Qualitative studies were included if they provided information on participant preferences or feasibility. Case reports were excluded due to their low level of evidence. The review followed the Cochrane Collaboration Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. This guideline provides a comprehensive framework for implementing PC programs to control T. solium taeniasis, addressing critical outcomes, operational issues, and evidence gaps to improve public health in endemic areas.
